slides.title: Bridging Barriers
slides.subtitle: Aural cues, codeswitching, and vocabulary learning for visually impaired learners

articleDetails.authors: Areen Badri, Suzanne Graham & Pengchong Zhang

blocks.text: Today’s purpose: examine the article’s evidence, question its implications, and connect the findings to our English-teaching context.

slides.notes: Welcome the group. Remind participants that everyone has read the article and that the meeting is a conversation, not a lecture.

slides.title: Start with your reading
slides.subtitle: Before revisiting the study, surface the ideas participants brought with them.

items: Which claim, result, or example stayed with you after reading?
What did you find convincing, surprising, or difficult to interpret?
What question did you bring to this discussion?

blocks.text: Facilitation move: invite a brief round-robin, then group similar responses without evaluating them yet.

slides.notes: Allow a few seconds of quiet thinking before inviting responses. Make space for different interpretations and ask participants to refer to the article.

slides.title: What problem does the article address?

items.title: A teaching challenge
items.text: Language lessons can rely heavily on visual material, creating barriers for learners with visual impairment (VI).

items.title: A research gap
items.text: The authors identify a shortage of rigorous classroom research on effective foreign-language teaching for VI learners.

items.title: The central question
items.text: Can making spoken target words more noticeable, alongside an L1 explanation, improve L2 vocabulary learning?

blocks.text: Clarify the distinction between an accessible route to input and a learner’s level of language proficiency.

slides.notes: Ask participants how the research problem is framed and whose perspectives or classroom experiences are most visible in that framing.

slides.title: What did the researchers compare?

items.title: CS · Codeswitching
items.text: The teacher explains an English target word using the learners’ first language (Arabic) within an otherwise English lesson.

items.title: AIM · Aural Input Manipulation
items.text: Spoken input is manipulated to make selected language features more noticeable. Here, target words were made louder.

items.title: AIMCS
items.text: The target English word is made louder and is then explained in Arabic.

blocks.text: The experiment compared AIMCS with CS. It did not test AIM alone or include a no-treatment control group.

slides.notes: Check that the group distinguishes the broad idea of aural input manipulation from the specific increased-volume technique used in this experiment.

slides.title: How was the study conducted?

items: 32 Saudi female high-school EFL learners: 16 visually impaired and 16 sighted participants; Arabic was their first language.
Participants were low-intermediate learners, aged 16–20, with six years of English schooling.
Across six 50-minute sessions, each learner experienced both CS and AIMCS conditions with counterbalanced target words.
Learning was measured through immediate and two-week delayed vocabulary meaning-recognition tests.

blocks.text: Evidence check: Which design choices strengthen the comparison, and which features limit how widely we can generalize the results?

slides.notes: Emphasize that the participants were school learners, not university students. Invite the group to comment on sample size, setting, measures, and the absence of an AIM-only condition.

slides.title: What did the results show?

items.title: Short-term learning
items.text: AIMCS produced significantly better short-term vocabulary learning than CS for both VI and sighted learners.

items.title: Delayed learning
items.text: The AIMCS advantage over CS was not maintained at the two-week delayed post-test.

items.title: Learner differences
items.text: VI learners benefited more overall in the short term; listening proficiency was especially relevant to VI learners’ gains.

items.title: Existing vocabulary
items.text: Learners with lower pre-existing vocabulary knowledge made greater gains, regardless of group or condition.

blocks.text: Interpretation check: the results support a short-term advantage in this study—not a claim that AIMCS improves long-term retention.

slides.notes: Ask participants to distinguish the reported findings from the authors’ explanations for those findings. If needed, revisit the article’s results tables.

slides.title: How strong is the argument?

items: How well do the measures capture vocabulary knowledge and retention?
What can—and can’t—we conclude when AIMCS is compared with CS but not with AIM alone or a no-treatment group?
Are the authors’ explanations (noticing, L1 mediation, sensory compensation) demonstrated by the results or offered as interpretations?
Which limitations most affect the study’s conclusions or relevance to other learners?

blocks.text: Facilitation move: ask ‘What in the article makes you say that?’ and invite a different reading before moving on.

slides.notes: Encourage evidence-based critique rather than a simple vote for or against the article. Give participants time to locate supporting passages.

slides.title: What might this mean for our classrooms?

items: How do we currently make important vocabulary noticeable in listening activities?
When might an Arabic explanation support learning, and when might it be less useful?
How can we create repeated, meaningful and productive encounters that support longer-term retention?
How could these ideas be adapted inclusively for visually impaired university learners?

blocks.text: The study involved low-intermediate Saudi high-school learners. Treat university-level applications as informed possibilities, not tested outcomes.

slides.notes: Invite participants to offer one practical adaptation and identify what evidence or learner feedback they would want before adopting it.

slides.title: One insight, one next step

items: What is one idea from the article you will continue thinking about?
What is one question or classroom practice you would like to explore further?

blocks.text: Take-away: the article offers evidence for an aural, inclusive approach to short-term vocabulary learning, while highlighting the need to plan for retention and further research.

slides.notes: Close by asking participants for a concise takeaway. Thank them, and note any questions or follow-up actions for the next reading circle.
